stimulus.text:
Unemployment in the United States, as a share of the labor force (Bureau of Labor Statistics historical estimates):

| Year | 1929 | 1930 | 1931 | 1932 | 1933 | 1937 | 1938 | 1941 | 1942 |
| Unemployment | 3.2% | 8.7% | 15.9% | 23.6% | 24.9% | 14.3% | 19.0% | 9.9% | 4.7% |

Context: The 1920s were years of prosperity built on assembly-line production, radios, cars, and buying on credit, including buying stocks on margin. The stock market crashed in October 1929.
stimulus.source_note: Unemployment figures are Bureau of Labor Statistics historical estimates, as published in the Economic Report of the President (Table B-22). Context drawn from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topics 7.7 and 7.9.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded paraphrases, tables, and photographs (see source_note)
stem: Which explanation of the Depression best fits the table and its context?

options.text: One cause alone explains the crash: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff
options.misconception: The tariff came in 1930, after the 1929 crash, so it cannot be the only cause.

options.text: The crash was caused only by falling farm prices in 1929
options.misconception: Farm distress was one cause among several, not the only cause.

options.text: The Depression was caused only by the New Deal's programs
options.misconception: The New Deal began in 1933, years after the crash and the rise in unemployment.

options.text: Several causes combined: speculation, weak banks, and falling demand

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 deepened the slump but followed the crash.
rationales.B: Background from the books: farm distress mattered, but so did speculation, weak banks, and falling demand.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the New Deal answered the Depression; it began four years after the crash.
rationales.D: The context names buying stocks on margin, and the table's long climb shows a system-wide collapse, not a single shock.
rationales.general:
1. Check each single-cause answer against the dates in the stimulus.
2. The tariff came in 1930 and the New Deal in 1933, both after the 1929 crash.
3. Background: the books list several causes, including speculation, fragile banks, and falling demand.
4. A collapse that climbs from 3.2 to 24.9 percent over four years fits many causes at once.
Remember: a four-year collapse usually has more than one cause.
